also.hook: Ritualo sits at a position that barely existed five years ago: the combined Chief Data and AI Officer function inside a cabinet-level foreign policy agency. Her career was built entirely on the federal data and performance management side, monitoring and evaluation, division chief, deputy CDAO, making her one of the few senior government AI officers whose path to the role ran through data governance and program evaluation rather than technology procurement.

profiles.hook: Amba Kak is co-executive director of the AI Now Institute, where she works on policy responses to the concentration of power in the AI industry. She trained as a lawyer in India, then won a Rhodes Scholarship to Oxford, where she earned a Master's in Law and an MSc in the Social Science of the Internet. Early in her career she advised India's telecom regulator, TRAI, on net neutrality, then worked as a global policy advisor at Mozilla. She later joined the US Federal Trade Commission as a senior advisor on AI, a role she held through 2022, before returning to lead the AI Now Institute alongside Sarah Myers West. Since then she has testified before Congress, represented civil society at the UK's first AI Safety Summit, and addressed the UN General Assembly on AI governance, arguing that unchecked AI development is concentrating power in a small number of technology companies.

profiles.hook: David Sacks is a Silicon Valley entrepreneur and venture capitalist who spent over 25 years building and investing in technology companies before taking on a formal role in AI and crypto policy. Born in South Africa, he came up in Silicon Valley as PayPal's first product leader and chief operating officer, then founded the enterprise social network Yammer, which Microsoft acquired for 1.2 billion dollars in 2012. He went on to found Craft Ventures, a San Francisco venture capital firm, and became an early investor in companies including Airbnb, SpaceX and Palantir, while co-hosting the widely followed All-In podcast. In December 2024, President-elect Trump named him White House AI and Crypto Czar, a newly created post directing administration policy on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency and chairing the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. After roughly 130 days in that day-to-day role, he stepped down in March 2026 and was named co-chair of PCAST alongside OSTP Director Michael Kratsios, broadening his advisory portfolio to the wider range of federal science and technology policy.

profiles.hook: Helen Toner is executive director of Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, where she studies the security implications of AI, export controls, and US-China technology competition. Born and raised in Australia, she holds a BSc in chemical engineering from the University of Melbourne before moving into technology policy, first as a senior research analyst at Open Philanthropy advising on AI grantmaking, then as a research affiliate at Oxford's Centre for the Governance of AI, spending nine months in Beijing studying China's AI ecosystem. In September 2021 she joined OpenAI's board of directors. She left the board in November 2023, after the board's brief removal and reinstatement of CEO Sam Altman, a crisis in which she said the board had been kept in the dark about matters including the launch of ChatGPT and Altman's ownership stake in the OpenAI Startup Fund. She has since testified before multiple congressional committees on AI policy and continues to lead CSET's research program.

profiles.hook: Jack Clark is a co-founder of Anthropic who began his career as a technical journalist covering distributed systems, quantum computing and AI for Bloomberg Businessweek and The Register. In September 2016 he joined OpenAI, where he became policy director and helped build the organization's early approach to AI policy. In 2017 he became a founding member of Stanford's AI Index, the annual report that tracks the state of global AI progress, and later served as an inaugural member of the US National AI Advisory Committee. In 2021 he co-founded Anthropic and led its policy work as co-founder and head of policy, while continuing to publish Import AI, a weekly newsletter on AI research and policy now read by more than 100,000 subscribers. He has testified before Congress on the importance of democratic countries leading AI development. In March 2026, he moved into a new role as Anthropic's Head of Public Benefit, leading the newly formed Anthropic Institute, a research effort on AI's societal, economic and legal impact.

profiles.hook: Joy Buolamwini is a computer scientist whose research exposed how commercial facial recognition systems perform far worse on darker skinned faces than lighter skinned ones. While a graduate researcher at the MIT Media Lab, she found that some facial analysis software failed to detect her own face until she put on a white mask, an experience that led her to start systematically testing commercial systems for bias. In 2016 she founded the Algorithmic Justice League to combine research, art, and advocacy against harmful bias in AI systems. Her 2018 study Gender Shades, co-authored with Timnit Gebru, tested facial analysis products from IBM, Microsoft, and Face++ using a new benchmark built from images of parliamentarians in African and European countries, and found error rates for darker skinned women far higher than for lighter skinned men. She holds a bachelor's degree in computer science from the Georgia Institute of Technology, studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, and earned her PhD from the MIT Media Lab. Her work has since informed congressional testimony on facial recognition technology, the 2020 documentary Coded Bias, and her 2023 book Unmasking AI.

profiles.hook: Margaret Mitchell is an AI researcher whose work focuses on documentation and transparency practices meant to make machine learning systems more accountable. Working across natural language processing and computer vision, she has held research roles at Microsoft Research, Google, and now Hugging Face. In 2018 she was the lead author of Model Cards for Model Reporting, a paper written with a team of Google and academic researchers, including Timnit Gebru, that proposed short standardized documents to accompany released machine learning models describing how they perform across different conditions and demographic groups. The model card format she helped design was later adopted widely across the AI industry. At Hugging Face she works on the company's Society and Ethics research efforts and contributes to open research initiatives such as the BigScience and BigCode workshops. Her research continues to center on practical tools, such as model documentation and bias evaluation methods, that let developers and the public better understand what a given AI system does and does not do well.

profiles.hook: Miles Brundage is an AI policy researcher who spent six years at OpenAI working on how the world should prepare for increasingly capable AI systems. He holds a BA in political science from George Washington University and a PhD in the Human and Social Dimensions of Science and Technology from Arizona State University, completed in 2019, with earlier stints at ARPA-E and the Institute for Human and Machine Cognition. From 2016 to 2018 he was a research fellow at Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute before joining OpenAI in 2018 as a research scientist on its policy team. Over six years there he rose to head of policy research and then senior advisor for AGI readiness, leading the company's external red-teaming program and developing its first system cards for documenting model capabilities. He left OpenAI in October 2024, saying he wanted to influence AI's development from outside industry, and went on to found AVERI, a nonprofit focused on independent AI policy research, while advising organizations including the Institute for Progress, CNAS, Epoch AI and RAND.

profiles.hook: Paul Scharre is a former Army Ranger turned defense policy analyst who leads work on autonomous weapons and AI strategy at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS). He served as a special operations reconnaissance team leader in the Army's 3rd Ranger Battalion, deploying multiple times to Iraq and Afghanistan, before moving into the Office of the Secretary of Defense. There he directed the working group that wrote DoD Directive 3000.09, the Pentagon's foundational policy on autonomy in weapons systems, and contributed to the 2010 Quadrennial Defense Review and the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance. He holds a PhD in war studies from King's College London and a master's and bachelor's from Washington University in St. Louis. At CNAS he wrote Army of None, a 2018 book on autonomous weapons that won the William E. Colby Award and was named one of Bill Gates' top five books of the year, and Four Battlegrounds, a 2023 book on the global contest for AI power that led to his inclusion on TIME's inaugural TIME100/AI list.

profiles.hook: Rumman Chowdhury is a data scientist who has built her career around auditing artificial intelligence systems for bias and holding the companies that deploy them accountable. She holds a PhD and led artificial intelligence ethics work at the consulting firm Accenture before joining Twitter, where she served as engineering director of the company's Machine Learning Ethics, Transparency and Accountability team and helped pioneer the use of algorithmic bias bounty programs, in which outside researchers are invited to find and report harms in a company's AI systems. She went on to found Humane Intelligence, a nonprofit that designs large scale, structured red teaming exercises to evaluate AI systems for fairness and safety in partnership with governments and industry. The Biden Administration appointed her the US Department of State's Science Envoy for Artificial Intelligence, a role in which she advises on AI governance issues internationally. Chowdhury stepped down as chief executive of Humane Intelligence in 2025 and remains an affiliate of Harvard's Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society.

profiles.hook: Sarah Myers West is co-executive director of the AI Now Institute, where her research examines how market incentives and infrastructure shape the societal impact of AI. She earned her PhD and Master's at the University of Southern California's Annenberg School, studying how technology companies act as political actors in global governance. She went on to serve as a senior advisor on AI at the US Federal Trade Commission, working on competition and data-privacy issues, while also holding a visiting research post at Northeastern University. At AI Now she has testified repeatedly before Congress, including the Senate Judiciary and Senate Banking Committees, on algorithmic accountability and AI market concentration, and has advised the UK government, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the City of New York. She is completing a book, Tracing Code, on the history of data capitalism, for University of California Press.

profiles.hook: Timnit Gebru is a computer scientist who has become one of the most prominent voices in AI ethics and accountability. She earned her PhD in computer vision from Stanford University, advised by Fei-Fei Li, after early work in circuit design and audio engineering at Apple. She then completed a postdoctoral fellowship in Microsoft Research's Fairness, Accountability, Transparency and Ethics group before joining Google in 2018, where she co-led the Ethical AI research team with Margaret Mitchell. Gebru left Google in December 2020 after a dispute over a research paper examining the risks of large language models, a departure that drew wide attention to tensions between AI ethics researchers and corporate priorities. In December 2021 she founded the Distributed AI Research Institute, an independent, interdisciplinary institute with researchers based across North America, Europe and Africa that studies the harms of current AI systems and researches alternative approaches. She also co-founded Black in AI, a nonprofit supporting Black researchers and students in artificial intelligence.
